title: Swordsman: Entropy-Driven Adaptive Block Partition for Efficient Diffusion Language Models
claim: Fixed-length blocks ignore uncertainty shifts and cut through coherent units; adapting block boundaries to entropy shifts aligns them with natural constituents.
layout: 2 stacked heatmap panels, top-to-bottom, yellow boxes highlight the compared region
description: Two vertically stacked heatmaps share a color scale on the right, labeled Entropy and running from dark blue (0) through pale yellow to red (10). The x-axis is token position (0–224) and the y-axis is inference step. Panel (a), Fast-dLLM (fixed block), has evenly spaced white dashed vertical lines marking fixed-length block boundaries. Panel (b), Swordsman (adaptive block), has irregularly spaced dashed lines placed at entropy shifts. White stars trace the decoding frontier in both panels. A red vertical stripe marks a high-entropy token at about position 46 in both. A bright yellow rectangle in each panel highlights the same region, roughly positions 82–168, so the reader can compare how blocks cut through or align with that region. Panel (b) finishes in fewer steps.
caption: Entropy evolution during decoding reveals semantic boundaries through shifts. Fast-dLLM (a) ignores entropy variance, applying predetermined fixed-length blocks that frequently fragment coherent constituents or merge semantically distinct ones, thereby degrading generation accuracy. Swordsman (b), however, leverages entropy shifts to adaptively align block boundaries with semantic constituents, partitioning at maximum shift points to achieve precise segmentation that yields better generations.
abstract: Block-wise decoding effectively improves the inference speed and quality in diffusion language models (DLMs) by combining inter-block sequential denoising and intra-block parallel unmasking. However, existing block-wise decoding methods typically partition blocks in a rigid and fixed manner, which inevitably fragments complete semantic or syntactic constituents, leading to suboptimal performance. Inspired by the entropy reduction hypothesis (ERH), we recognize that constituent boundaries offer greater opportunities for uncertainty reduction, which motivates us to employ entropy analysis for identifying constituent boundaries. Therefore, we propose Swordsman, an entropy-driven adaptive block-wise decoding framework for DLMs. Swordsman adaptively partitions blocks by identifying entropy shifts between adjacent tokens to better align with semantic or syntactic constituent boundaries. In addition, Swordsman dynamically adjusts unmasking thresholds conditioned on the real-time unmasking status within a block, further improving both efficiency and stability. As a training-free framework, supported by KV Cache, Swordsman demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across extensive evaluations.
